Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The main action is forwarding the inspection packet to the facilities desk before noon so they can use the notes when they plan the next service visit. I am forwarding the packet because the maintenance calendar is being set this week, and the desk asked for a record of what we actually checked. The packet has the room sketch, the fan labels, the reading sheet, and a short note from Mara at the front office. I checked that each page was in the folder before I left the workshop, and the original reading sheet stays in the blue binder by the tool cabinet.

We began at eight fifteen after the night shift had moved its carts away from the intake wall. The workshop was open, but no cutting or sanding was underway during the check. The east door was closed, and the high window above the sink was open about a hand width. I noted both details because the room does not behave the same way when the doors are left open. The wall fan is marked F2, and the ceiling extractor is marked E1. Those labels match the sketch from last autumn, although the tape on the extractor switch is peeling at the lower corner.

Mara unlocked the narrow electrical cupboard and waited while I checked the meter against the small reference unit from the stores shelf. The meter display came on without a warning symbol, and the reference unit was within its date for the check. I wrote down the serial numbers rather than relying on the labels because the label on the meter case has a crease through the final digit. The serial ending forty-eight belongs to the meter, and the unit ending eleven belongs to the reference device. I returned both units to Mara before we started taking readings. She kept the cupboard key on her ring throughout.

We took readings at the marked floor position near the centre bench and at the two pencil marks beside the paint rack. I used the same height for each position and waited for the display to settle before recording a number. The centre bench point was checked twice because a trolley passed behind me during the first reading. The two results are written separately on the sheet, and I have not averaged them. The paint rack points were checked once each. The north mark is closer to the supply grille, and the south mark is beside the lower storage shelf. The grille itself was clear, but a paper tag was tied to its outer edge.

Mara said, “Please leave the tag in place because it belongs to the inventory check, and I will remove it after the count.” I left it there and added the note to the sketch. The tag did not cover the grille opening, but it could be seen from the floor mark. I did not move the storage shelf or any of the tools around it. The workshop lead, Jon, said, “If the loading door is open, the draft reaches the paint rack first.” The loading door remained shut while we were there, and Jon was speaking about the usual afternoon deliveries rather than the morning check.

Then there is the numbered section for the packet:
1. The room sketch has the intake wall, the sink window, the east door, the loading door, and the three reading positions marked in pencil.
2. The reading sheet lists the time, the position, and the displayed value in separate columns, and it keeps the two centre bench entries on separate lines.
3. The equipment note gives the meter and reference unit serial endings and says that the reference unit was within its date.
These are descriptions of what is in the folder, not a summary of what the readings mean. I checked that the pages are in the same order as the index and that the sketch can be read without removing it from the clear sleeve.

There is one condition that matters for the later comparison: if the exterior wind is above twenty-five kilometres per hour when the next check is done, the facilities desk should keep that day's readings separate from these morning readings and note the wind speed on its sheet. That condition is written in the margin of the reading sheet and repeated in the cover note. It is not a request to cancel the next check. The weather board at the workshop entrance showed a lower wind speed at nine o'clock, but I did not copy that figure into the comparison note because the condition concerns the day of the next check.

Before leaving, I asked Mara whether the service calendar had a fixed date. She said the desk was collecting availability and had not set one. She asked me to send the packet by email as well as putting a copy in the internal tray. I told her I could forward the scanned pages after checking that the serial endings were legible. The scan is not attached to this account because I made it after returning to the office. The folder itself remains with me until the facilities desk confirms it has received the paper copy and the email.

At eleven twenty, I checked the scan against the folder and could read all three serial endings without enlarging the image. The tag beside the grille is visible in the room sketch note, and the two centre bench readings remain separate in the scanned sheet. I am forwarding the packet now to the facilities desk with Mara copied on the email, and the paper copy is in the internal tray marked facilities. The calendar date is still unset, and the next comparison will depend on the wind condition written in the margin. I have not added a proposed service date or an interpretation of the readings to the packet."}]
